question.:question/problem:
Consider the following first-order linear ODE for the function $y=y(x):$

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+\left(4\right)\cdot y=4 e^{- 2 x}
$$

Write the equation in the form $\frac{d}{dx}(yI(x))=I(x)Q(x),$ where $I(x)$ is an integrating factor.
question.:question/worked-solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=4$ and $Q(x)=4 e^{- 2 x}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & =e^{\int P(x)\,dx} \\  & =e^{\int \left(4\right)\,dx} \\  & =e^{4 x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)=e^{4 x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x)\cdot \left(\frac{dy}{dx}+\left(4\right)\cdot y\right) & =I(x)\cdot \left(4 e^{- 2 x}\right) \\ I(x)\frac{dy}{dx}+P(x)I(x)y & =4 e^{2 x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dx}\left(y\cdot \left(e^{4 x}\right)\right) & =4 e^{2 x}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the following first-order linear ODE for the function $y=y(x):$

$$
\left(x\right)\cdot \frac{dy}{dx}+\left(4\right)\cdot y=1
$$

Write the equation in the form $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(yI(x))=I(x)Q(x),$ where $I(x)$ is an integrating factor.

Assume $x>0$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we write the equation in standard form. This gives

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+\left(\frac{4}{x}\right)\cdot y=\frac{1}{x}.
$$

This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{4}{x}$ and $Q(x)=\frac{1}{x}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & =e^{\int P(x)\,dx} \\  & =e^{\int \left(\frac{4}{x}\right)\,dx} \\  & =e^{4 \ln{\left(x \right)}} \\  & =e^{\ln \left(x^{4}\right)} \\  & =x^{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)=x^{4}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x)\cdot \left(\frac{dy}{dx}+\left(\frac{4}{x}\right)\cdot y\right) & =I(x)\cdot \left(\frac{1}{x}\right) \\ I(x)\frac{dy}{dx}+P(x)I(x)y & =\left(x^{4}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x)):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dx}\left(y\cdot \left(x^{4}\right)\right) & =\left(x^{4}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the following first-order linear ODE for the function $y=y(x)$:

$$
\left(2 x\right)\cdot \frac{dy}{dx}+\left(2\right)\cdot y=6 x y - 2 \cos{\left(x \right)}
$$

Write the equation in the form $\frac{d}{dx}(yI(x))=I(x)Q(x)$, where $I(x)$ is an integrating factor.

Assume $x>0$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Collect the $y$-terms on the left:

$$
\left(2 x\right)\cdot \frac{dy}{dx}-\left(6 x - 2\right)\cdot y=- 2 \cos{\left(x \right)}
$$

First, we write the equation in standard form. This gives

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}-\left(3 - \frac{1}{x}\right)\cdot y=- \frac{\cos{\left(x \right)}}{x}.
$$

This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=-3 + \frac{1}{x}$ and $Q(x)=- \frac{\cos{\left(x \right)}}{x}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & =e^{\int P(x)\,dx} \\  & =e^{\int \left(-3 + \frac{1}{x}\right)\,dx} \\  & =e^{- 3 x + \ln{\left(x \right)}} \\  & =x e^{- 3 x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)=x e^{- 3 x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x)\cdot \left(\frac{dy}{dx}-\left(3 - \frac{1}{x}\right)\cdot y\right) & =I(x)\cdot \left(- \frac{\cos{\left(x \right)}}{x}\right) \\ I(x)\frac{dy}{dx}+P(x)I(x)y & =- e^{- 3 x} \cos{\left(x \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dx}\left(y\cdot \left(x e^{- 3 x}\right)\right) & =- e^{- 3 x} \cos{\left(x \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

\left(2 x\right)\cdot \frac{dy}{dx}+\left(4 x + 4\right)\cdot y=- 6 \cos{\left(x \right)}

\frac{dy}{dx}+\left(2 + \frac{2}{x}\right)\cdot y=- \frac{3 \cos{\left(x \right)}}{x}.

question.:question/problem:
Consider the differential equation
$\frac{dy}{dx} - 6y = x^{2}e^{6x}$.
Select the correct options below.
An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x) =$ {{field-1}}.

The general solution is given by $y(x) =$ {{field-2}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=-6$ and $Q(x)={x}^{2}{e}^{6x}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int -6\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-6x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={e}^{-6x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{-6x}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-6y) & ={e}^{-6x}\cdot {x}^{2}{e}^{6x} \\ {e}^{-6x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-6{e}^{-6x}\cdot y & ={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x))$ and carry out the integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{-6x}) & ={x}^{2} \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{-6x})\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ y{e}^{-6x} & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+C \\ y & =\frac{{x}^{3}{e}^{6x}}{3}+C{e}^{6x}\end{aligned}
$$

\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)

with $P(x)=-4$ and $Q(x)=2{e}^{x}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

question.:question/problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{5}{x}y=\frac{{e}^{3x}}{{x}^{5}},\,x>0.
$$

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The general solution is given by $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{5}{x}$ and $Q(x)=\frac{{e}^{3x}}{{x}^{5}}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,dx} \\  & ={e}^{\int (5/x)\,dx} \\  & ={e}^{5\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{5})} \\  & ={x}^{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={x}^{5}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{5}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{5}{x}y) & ={x}^{5}\cdot \frac{{e}^{3x}}{{x}^{5}} \\ {x}^{5}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+5{x}^{4}\cdot y & ={e}^{3x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x))$ and carry out the integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dx}(y{x}^{5})\,dx & =\int {e}^{3x}\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{5} & =\frac{{e}^{3x}}{3}+C \\ y & =\frac{\frac{{e}^{3x}}{3}+C}{{x}^{5}}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the differential equation
$\frac{dy}{dx} + \frac{5}{x}y = 3, x > 0$.

Select the correct options below:

An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x) =$ {{field-1}}.

The general solution is given by $y(x) =$ {{field-2}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{5}{x}$ and $Q(x)=3.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,dx} \\  & ={e}^{\int (5/x)\,dx} \\  & ={e}^{5\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{5})} \\  & ={x}^{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={x}^{5}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{5}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{5}{x}y) & ={x}^{5}\cdot 3 \\ {x}^{5}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+5{x}^{4}y & =3{x}^{5}\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dx}(y{x}^{5})\,dx & =\int 3{x}^{5}\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{5} & =\frac{3{x}^{6}}{6}+C \\ y & =\frac{x}{2}+\frac{C}{{x}^{5}}.\end{aligned}

First divide the equation by $5$ to write it in standard form.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{5}y=\frac{6x}{5}
$$

This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{1}{5}$ and $Q(x)=\frac{6x}{5}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int 1/5\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{x/5}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={e}^{x/5}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x/5}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{5}y) & ={e}^{x/5}\cdot \frac{6x}{5} \\ {e}^{x/5}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{5}{e}^{x/5}\cdot y & =\frac{6x}{5}{e}^{x/5}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x))$ and carry out the integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{x/5}) & =\frac{6x}{5}{e}^{x/5} \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{x/5})\text{d}x & =\int \frac{6x}{5}{e}^{x/5}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this integral, we integrate by parts.

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int {u}^{′}v\,\text{d}x
$$

Let $u=x,{u}^{′}=1,{v}^{′}={e}^{x/5},$ and $v=5{e}^{x/5}.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y{e}^{x/5} & =\int \frac{6x}{5}{e}^{x/5}\,\text{d}x \\ y{e}^{x/5} & =\frac{6}{5}\left(x(5{e}^{x/5})-\int 5{e}^{x/5}\,\text{d}x\right) \\ y{e}^{x/5} & =6x{e}^{x/5}-6\int {e}^{x/5}\,\text{d}x \\ y{e}^{x/5} & =6x{e}^{x/5}-30{e}^{x/5}+C \\ y{e}^{x/5} & =6(x-5){e}^{x/5}+C \\ y & =6(x - 5) + Ce^{-x/5}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the following initial value problem.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\left(2\right)y=10,\quad y(0)=6
$$

Select the correct options below.

An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

The solution to the initial value problem is $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x),
$$

with $P(x)=2$ and $Q(x)=10.$

We compute an integrating factor using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & =e^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & =e^{\int 2\,\text{d}x} \\  & =e^{2 x}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)=e^{2 x}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}e^{2 x}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y) & =e^{2 x}\cdot 10 \\ e^{2 x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2 e^{2 x}y & =10 e^{2 x} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(ye^{2 x}) & =10 e^{2 x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(ye^{2 x})\,\text{d}x & =\int 10 e^{2 x}\,\text{d}x \\ ye^{2 x} & =10\left(\frac{1}{2} e^{2 x}\right)+C \\ ye^{2 x} & =5 e^{2 x}+C \\ y & =\left(C + 5 e^{2 x}\right) e^{- 2 x}\end{aligned}
$$

This is the general solution. To find the value of $C$ corresponding to the specific solution, we apply the initial condition $y(0)=6$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =\frac{(5 e^{2 (0)})+C}{(e^{2 (0)})} \\ 6 & =\frac{5+C}{1} \\ C & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=5 + e^{- 2 x}.
$$

The first step is to write the equation in standard form,

$$
\begin{aligned}x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y & =12 x^{2} \\ \frac{1}{x}\left(x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y\right) & =\frac{1}{x}\cdot 12 x^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}y & =12 x\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x),
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{2}{x}$ and $Q(x)=12 x.$

We compute an integrating factor using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & =e^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & =e^{\int \frac{2}{x}\,\text{d}x} \\  & =e^{2 \ln{\left(x \right)}} \\  & =x^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)=x^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}x^{2}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}y) & =x^{2}\cdot 12 x \\ x^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2 xy & =12 x^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(yx^{2}) & =12 x^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(yx^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int 12 x^{3}\,\text{d}x \\ yx^{2} & =3 x^{4}+C \\ y & =\frac{C + 3 x^{4}}{x^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

This is the general solution. To find the value of $C$ corresponding to the specific solution, we apply the initial condition $y(1)=6$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & =\frac{(3 (1)^{4})+C}{((1)^{2})} \\ 6 & =\frac{3+C}{1} \\ C & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$

$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x),
$$

with $P(x)=x^{2}$ and $Q(x)=5 x^{2}.$

We compute an integrating factor using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & =e^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & =e^{\int x^{2}\,\text{d}x} \\  & =e^{\frac{x^{3}}{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)=e^{\frac{x^{3}}{3}}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}e^{\frac{x^{3}}{3}}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+x^{2}y) & =e^{\frac{x^{3}}{3}}\cdot 5 x^{2} \\ e^{\frac{x^{3}}{3}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+x^{2} e^{\frac{x^{3}}{3}}y & =5 x^{2} e^{\frac{x^{3}}{3}} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(ye^{\frac{x^{3}}{3}}) & =5 x^{2} e^{\frac{x^{3}}{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x,$ making use of the substitution $u=\frac{x^{3}}{3}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(ye^{\frac{x^{3}}{3}})\,\text{d}x & =\int 5 x^{2} e^{\frac{x^{3}}{3}}\,\text{d}x \\ ye^{\frac{x^{3}}{3}} & =\int 5e^u\,\text{d}u \\ ye^{\frac{x^{3}}{3}} & =5e^u+C \\ ye^{\frac{x^{3}}{3}} & =5 e^{\frac{x^{3}}{3}}+C \\ y & =\left(C + 5 e^{\frac{x^{3}}{3}}\right) e^{- \frac{x^{3}}{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

This is the general solution. To find the value of $C$ corresponding to the specific solution, we apply the initial condition $y(0)=3$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =\frac{(5 e^{\frac{(0)^{3}}{3}})+C}{(e^{\frac{(0)^{3}}{3}})} \\ 3 & =\frac{5+C}{1} \\ C & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=5 - 2 e^{- \frac{x^{3}}{3}}.
$$

$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)=e^{\frac{x^{2}}{10}}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}e^{\frac{x^{2}}{10}}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{x}{5}y) & =e^{\frac{x^{2}}{10}}\cdot \frac{6 x}{5} \\ e^{\frac{x^{2}}{10}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{x e^{\frac{x^{2}}{10}}}{5}y & =\frac{6 x e^{\frac{x^{2}}{10}}}{5} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(ye^{\frac{x^{2}}{10}}) & =\frac{6 x e^{\frac{x^{2}}{10}}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(ye^{\frac{x^{2}}{10}})\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{6 x e^{\frac{x^{2}}{10}}}{5}\,\text{d}x \\ ye^{\frac{x^{2}}{10}} & =\int 6e^u\,\text{d}u \\ ye^{\frac{x^{2}}{10}} & =6e^u+C \\ ye^{\frac{x^{2}}{10}} & =6 e^{\frac{x^{2}}{10}}+C \\ y & =\left(C + 6 e^{\frac{x^{2}}{10}}\right) e^{- \frac{x^{2}}{10}}\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem: Find $f_x(x,y)$ for $f(x,y)=\tan{\left(\ln{\left(x + y + 2 \right)} \right)}$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Treat $y$ as constant and differentiate with respect to $x$. Apply the chain rule, and the sum and constant multiple rules where needed.

$$
\begin{aligned}
u&=x + y + 2\\
\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}&=1\\
\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\tan(\ln u)&=\sec^2(\ln u)\cdot\frac{1}{u}\cdot\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\\
f_x(x,y)&=\left(\frac{\sec^{2}{\left(\ln{\left(u \right)} \right)}}{u}\right)\cdot\left(1\right)\\
&=\frac{\sec^{2}{\left(\ln{\left(x + y + 2 \right)} \right)}}{x + y + 2}
\end{aligned}
$$

These derivatives apply for $x + y + 2>0$ and $\cos(\ln(x + y + 2))\ne0$.

question.:question/problem: Find $f_x(x,y)$ for $f(x,y)=- y \ln{\left(x \right)} + e^{- 2 x^{3} y}$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Treat $y$ as constant and differentiate with respect to $x$. Apply the chain rule, and the sum and constant multiple rules where needed.

$$
\begin{aligned}
u&=- 2 x^{3} y\\
\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}&=- 6 x^{2} y\\
\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(e^{u}\right)&=\left(e^{u}\right)\cdot\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\\
\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(- y \ln{\left(x \right)}\right)&=- \frac{y}{x}\\
f_x(x,y)&=\left(e^{u}\right)\cdot\left(- 6 x^{2} y\right)+\left(- \frac{y}{x}\right)\\
&=- 6 x^{2} y e^{- 2 x^{3} y} - \frac{y}{x}
\end{aligned}
$$

These derivatives apply for $x>0$.

question.:question/problem: Find $f_x(x,y)$ for $f(x,y)=- x y + \ln{\left(- 2 x y \right)}$.

Treat $y$ as constant and differentiate with respect to $x$. Apply the chain rule, and the sum and constant multiple rules where needed.

$$
\begin{aligned}

\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(\ln{\left(u \right)}\right)&=\left(\frac{1}{u}\right)\cdot\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\\

question.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y)=\arctan{\left(x^{2} y \right)}$, evaluate $f_y(2,-1)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Treat $x$ as constant and differentiate with respect to $y$. Apply the chain rule, and the sum and constant multiple rules where needed.

$$
\begin{aligned}
u&=x^{2} y\\
\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}&=x^{2}\\
\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(\arctan{\left(u \right)}\right)&=\left(\frac{1}{u^{2} + 1}\right)\cdot\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\\
f_y(x,y)&=\left(\frac{1}{u^{2} + 1}\right)\cdot\left(x^{2}\right)\\
&=\frac{x^{2}}{x^{4} y^{2} + 1}
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute $x=2$ and $y=-1$ after differentiating. The inner input is

$$
u_0=\left(2\right)^{2} \left(-1\right)=-4.
$$

Using this value in the chain factors gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_y(2,-1)&=\left(\frac{1}{u_0^{2} + 1}\right)\cdot\left(4\right)\\
&=\left(\frac{1}{17}\right)\cdot\left(4\right)\\
&=\frac{4}{17}.
\end{aligned}
$$

These derivatives apply for all real $x,y$.

question.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y)=2 \sqrt{x} y^{2} + \sqrt{x - y}$, evaluate $f_y(4,3)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Treat $x$ as constant and differentiate with respect to $y$. Apply the chain rule, and the sum and constant multiple rules where needed.

$$
\begin{aligned}
u&=x - y\\
\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}&=-1\\
\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(\sqrt{u}\right)&=\left(\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{u}}\right)\cdot\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\\
\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(2 \sqrt{x} y^{2}\right)&=4 \sqrt{x} y\\
f_y(x,y)&=\left(\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{u}}\right)\cdot\left(-1\right)+\left(4 \sqrt{x} y\right)\\
&=4 \sqrt{x} y - \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{x - y}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute $x=4$ and $y=3$ after differentiating. The inner input is

$$
u_0=\left(4\right) - \left(3\right)=1.
$$

Using this value in the chain factors gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_y(4,3)&=\left(\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{u_0}}\right)\cdot\left(-1\right)+\left(24\right)\\
&=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\cdot\left(-1\right)+\left(24\right)\\
&=\frac{47}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

These derivatives apply for $x>0$ and $x - y>0$.

question.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y)=2 x^{2} y^{2} - \cos{\left(2 x y \right)}$, evaluate $f_x(\frac{\pi}{4},2)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Treat $y$ as constant and differentiate with respect to $x$. Apply the chain rule, and the sum and constant multiple rules where needed.

$$
\begin{aligned}
u&=2 x y\\
\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}&=2 y\\
\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(- \cos{\left(u \right)}\right)&=\left(\sin{\left(u \right)}\right)\cdot\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\\
\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(2 x^{2} y^{2}\right)&=4 x y^{2}\\
f_x(x,y)&=\left(\sin{\left(u \right)}\right)\cdot\left(2 y\right)+\left(4 x y^{2}\right)\\
&=4 x y^{2} + 2 y \sin{\left(2 x y \right)}
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute $x=\frac{\pi}{4}$ and $y=2$ after differentiating. The inner input is

$$
u_0=2 \left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) \left(2\right)=\pi.
$$

Using this value in the chain factors gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x(\frac{\pi}{4},2)&=\left(\sin{\left(u_0 \right)}\right)\cdot\left(4\right)+\left(4 \pi\right)\\
&=\left(0\right)\cdot\left(4\right)+\left(4 \pi\right)\\
&=4 \pi.
\end{aligned}
$$

These derivatives apply for all real $x,y$.

question.:question/worked-solution:
Treat $y$ as constant and differentiate with respect to $x$. Apply the chain rule, and the sum and constant multiple rules where needed.

$$
\begin{aligned}
u&=2 x^{2} + y\\
\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}&=4 x\\
\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\ln(1+e^u)&=\frac{1}{1+e^u}\cdot e^u\cdot\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\\
\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(2 x^{2} y\right)&=4 x y\\
f_x(x,y)&=\left(\frac{e^{u}}{e^{u} + 1}\right)\cdot\left(4 x\right)+\left(4 x y\right)\\
&=4 x y + \frac{4 x e^{2 x^{2} + y}}{e^{2 x^{2} + y} + 1}
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute $x=-1$ and $y=1$ after differentiating. The inner input is

$$
u_0=2 \left(-1\right)^{2} + \left(1\right)=3.
$$

Using this value in the chain factors gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x(-1,1)&=\left(\frac{e^{u_0}}{e^{u_0} + 1}\right)\cdot\left(-4\right)+\left(-4\right)\\
&=\left(\frac{e^{3}}{1 + e^{3}}\right)\cdot\left(-4\right)+\left(-4\right)\\
&=\frac{4 \left(- 2 e^{3} - 1\right)}{1 + e^{3}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Treat $x$ as constant and differentiate with respect to $y$. Apply the chain rule, and the sum and constant multiple rules where needed.

$$
\begin{aligned}
u&=2 x^{2} + y\\
\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}&=1\\
\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\ln(1+e^u)&=\frac{1}{1+e^u}\cdot e^u\cdot\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\\
\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(2 x^{2} y\right)&=2 x^{2}\\
f_y(x,y)&=\left(\frac{e^{u}}{e^{u} + 1}\right)\cdot\left(1\right)+\left(2 x^{2}\right)\\
&=2 x^{2} + \frac{e^{2 x^{2} + y}}{e^{2 x^{2} + y} + 1}
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute $x=-1$ and $y=1$ after differentiating. The inner input is

$$
u_0=2 \left(-1\right)^{2} + \left(1\right)=3.
$$

Using this value in the chain factors gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_y(-1,1)&=\left(\frac{e^{u_0}}{e^{u_0} + 1}\right)\cdot\left(1\right)+\left(2\right)\\
&=\left(\frac{e^{3}}{1 + e^{3}}\right)\cdot\left(1\right)+\left(2\right)\\
&=\frac{2 + 3 e^{3}}{1 + e^{3}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

These derivatives apply for all real $x,y$.

Treat $y$ as constant and differentiate with respect to $x$. Apply the chain rule, and the sum and constant multiple rules where needed.

$$
\begin{aligned}
u&=- x y\\
\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}&=- y\\

f_x(x,y)&=\left(\frac{e^{u}}{e^{u} + 1}\right)\cdot\left(- y\right)+\left(y^{2}\right)\\

\end{aligned}
$$

$$
u_0=- \left(2\right) \left(1\right)=-2.

Using this value in the chain factors gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x(2,1)&=\left(\frac{e^{u_0}}{e^{u_0} + 1}\right)\cdot\left(-1\right)+\left(1\right)\\
&=\left(\frac{1}{\left(e^{-2} + 1\right) e^{2}}\right)\cdot\left(-1\right)+\left(1\right)\\
&=\frac{e^{2}}{1 + e^{2}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
u&=- x y\\
\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}&=- x\\

f_y(x,y)&=\left(\frac{e^{u}}{e^{u} + 1}\right)\cdot\left(- x\right)+\left(2 x y\right)\\
&=2 x y - \frac{x e^{- x y}}{1 + e^{- x y}}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
u_0=- \left(2\right) \left(1\right)=-2.

\begin{aligned}
f_y(2,1)&=\left(\frac{e^{u_0}}{e^{u_0} + 1}\right)\cdot\left(-2\right)+\left(4\right)\\
&=\left(\frac{1}{\left(e^{-2} + 1\right) e^{2}}\right)\cdot\left(-2\right)+\left(4\right)\\

question.:question/problem:
For the function

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{e^{- x y}}{x y - 1},
$$

the partial derivative with respect to $y$ is given by

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=\frac{h(x,y)e^{- x y}}{\left(x y - 1\right)^2}.
$$

Find $h(x,y)$, where $x y - 1\ne0$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Hold $x$ constant and differentiate with respect to $y$. Write $N=e^{- x y}$ and $D=x y - 1$. The component derivatives are

$$
\begin{aligned}
N_{y}&=- x e^{- x y}, \\
D_{y}&=x.
\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule differentiates the exponent first; its inner derivative is $- x$. Apply the quotient rule, keeping its subtraction and squared denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=\frac{N_{y}D-ND_{y}}{D^2} \\
&=\frac{\left(- x e^{- x y}\right)D-N\left(x\right)}{D^2} \\
&=\frac{e^{- x y}\left(- x^{2} y\right)}{\left(x y - 1\right)^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The last step factors the common nonzero exponential $e^{- x y}$ from the numerator. Comparing with the supplied form gives $h(x,y)=- x^{2} y$. These expressions apply where $x y - 1\ne0$.

For the function

f(x,y)=\frac{\sin{\left(x \right)} + \cos{\left(y \right)}}{\sin{\left(x \right)} - 2 \cos{\left(y \right)} + 1},
$$

the partial derivative with respect to $x$ is given by

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}=\frac{h(x,y)}{\left(\sin{\left(x \right)} - 2 \cos{\left(y \right)} + 1\right)^2}.
$$

Find $h(x,y)$, where $\sin{\left(x \right)} - 2 \cos{\left(y \right)} + 1\ne0$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Hold $y$ constant and differentiate with respect to $x$. Write $N=\sin{\left(x \right)} + \cos{\left(y \right)}$ and $D=\sin{\left(x \right)} - 2 \cos{\left(y \right)} + 1$. The component derivatives are

$$
\begin{aligned}
N_{x}&=\cos{\left(x \right)}, \\
D_{x}&=\cos{\left(x \right)}.
\end{aligned}
$$

 Apply the quotient rule, keeping its subtraction and squared denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}&=\frac{N_{x}D-ND_{x}}{D^2} \\
&=\frac{\left(\cos{\left(x \right)}\right)D-N\left(\cos{\left(x \right)}\right)}{D^2} \\
&=\frac{- 3 \cos{\left(x \right)} \cos{\left(y \right)} + \cos{\left(x \right)}}{\left(\sin{\left(x \right)} - 2 \cos{\left(y \right)} + 1\right)^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The last step distributes the subtraction and collects like terms. Comparing with the supplied form gives $h(x,y)=- 3 \cos{\left(x \right)} \cos{\left(y \right)} + \cos{\left(x \right)}$. These expressions apply where $\sin{\left(x \right)} - 2 \cos{\left(y \right)} + 1\ne0$.

$$
\begin{aligned}

 Apply the quotient rule, keeping its subtraction and squared denominator:

question.:question/problem:
For the function

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{- 3 x^{2} - y^{2} + 1}{e^{- x + y}},
$$

evaluate $\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}$ at the point $(1,-1)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Hold $x$ constant and differentiate with respect to $y$. Write $N=- 3 x^{2} - y^{2} + 1$ and $D=e^{- x + y}$. The component derivatives are

$$
\begin{aligned}
N_{y}&=- 2 y, \\
D_{y}&=e^{- x + y}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule differentiates the exponent first; its inner derivative is $1$. Apply the quotient rule, keeping its subtraction and squared denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=\frac{N_{y}D-ND_{y}}{D^2} \\
&=\frac{\left(- 2 y\right)D-N\left(e^{- x + y}\right)}{D^2} \\
&=\frac{3 x^{2} + y^{2} - 2 y - 1}{e^{- x + y}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The last step factors the common nonzero exponential $e^{- x + y}$ from the numerator. Cancel that factor with one copy in the squared denominator. Now substitute the point, after differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left.\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\right|_{(1,-1)}&=\frac{\left(2\right)\left(\frac{1}{e^{2}}\right)-\left(-3\right)\left(\frac{1}{e^{2}}\right)}{\left(\frac{1}{e^{2}}\right)^2} \\
&=5 e^{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

 These expressions apply where $e^{- x + y}\ne0$.

question.:question/problem: Find $f_{y}(x,y)$ for $f(x,y)=- 2 y- \sin{\left(x \right)}$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Differentiate with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as constant. Apply the sum and constant multiple rules term by term.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}(- 2 y) &=-2\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y) \\
&=-2\cdot \left(1\right) \\
&=-2\end{aligned}
$$

&=- \sin{\left(x \right)}\cdot \left(0\right) \\
&=0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore $f_{y}(x,y)=-2$.

question.:question/problem: Find $f_{y}(x,y)$ for $f(x,y)=\frac{y}{x}+\frac{x}{y^{2}}$, where $y\ne0$ and $x\ne0$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Differentiate with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as constant. Write reciprocal powers as negative powers, using $\frac{1}{y^n}=y^{-n}$ for positive $n$. Apply the sum and constant multiple rules term by term.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) &=\frac{1}{x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y) \\
&=\frac{1}{x}\cdot \left(1\right) \\
&=\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}\left(\frac{x}{y^{2}}\right) &=x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}\left(\frac{1}{y^{2}}\right) \\
&=x\cdot \left(- \frac{2}{y^{3}}\right) \\
&=- \frac{2 x}{y^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore $f_{y}(x,y)=- \frac{2 x}{y^{3}} + \frac{1}{x}$.

question.:question/problem: Given that $f(x,y)=\sin(4xy)$, which limit of a difference quotient represents $\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}$?
question.:question/worked-solution:
Hold $x$ constant. The definition gives

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(x,y+h)-f(x,y)}{h}.
$$

Replace every occurrence of $y$ by $(y+h)$ in the function, preserving each operator and its input:

$$
f(x,y+h)=\sin(4x(y+h)).
$$

$$

We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants:

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x^{2} y^{2}-2 x y) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x^{2} y^{2})-\frac{∂}{∂x}(2 x y) \\  & =y^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x^{2})-2 y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x) \\  & =y^{2}\cdot (2 x)-2 y\cdot (1) \\  & =2 x y^{2}-2 y\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(-3,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(-3,1)} & =2 (-3) (1)^{2}-2 (1) \\  & =-6-(2) \\  & =-8\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the general nonzero real solution to the differential equation

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}- 3 \cdot y=- 2 \cdot y^{2} \cdot e^{x}.
$$

Use the substitution $z=y^{-1}$.

Work on an interval where $x>0$. Choose constants and intervals on which the displayed expressions are real and finite.
question.:question/worked-solution:
This is a Bernoulli equation with

$$\begin{aligned}p(x)&=-3\\ q(x)&=- 2 \cdot e^{x}\\ n&=2.\end{aligned}$$

Divide by $y^{2}$ and set $z=y^{-1}$. The chain rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}=- \frac{1}{y^{2}}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.$$

Hence the linear equation in standard form is

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}+\left(3\right)z=2 \cdot e^{x}.$$

An integrating factor is

$$I(x)=e^{\int 3\,\mathrm{d}x}=e^{3 \cdot x}.$$

Multiplying through and using the product rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(e^{3 \cdot x}\,z\right)=2 \cdot e^{4 \cdot x}.$$

Integrating with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$e^{3 \cdot x}z=\frac{e^{4 \cdot x}}{2}+C.$$

Thus

$$z=C \cdot e^{- 3 \cdot x} + \frac{e^{x}}{2}.$$

Finally, substitute $z=y^{-1}$ and solve for $y$:

$$y=\frac{2 \cdot e^{3 \cdot x}}{2 \cdot C + e^{4 \cdot x}}.$$

Here $C$ is an arbitrary real constant; exclude singularities and restrict to the stated real intervals.

:answer-field/choices.:answer/value: y=\frac{4 \cdot e^{3 \cdot x}}{4 \cdot C - e^{4 \cdot x}}
y=\frac{2 \cdot e^{3 \cdot x}}{2 \cdot C + e^{4 \cdot x}}
y=\frac{3 \cdot e^{2 \cdot x}}{3 \cdot C - e^{3 \cdot x}}

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(e^{- \frac{3 \cdot x}{2}}\,z\right)=- e^{- \frac{3 \cdot x}{2}}.$$

Integrating with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$e^{- \frac{3 \cdot x}{2}}z=\frac{2 \cdot e^{- \frac{3 \cdot x}{2}}}{3}+C.$$

Thus

question.:question/worked-solution:
This is a Bernoulli equation with

$$\begin{aligned}p(x)&=1\\ q(x)&=- \left(x+6\right)\\ n&=3.\end{aligned}$$

Divide by $y^{3}$ and set $z=y^{-2}$. The chain rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}=- \frac{2}{y^{3}}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.$$

Hence the linear equation in standard form is

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}+\left(-2\right)z=2 \cdot \left(x+6\right).$$

An integrating factor is

$$I(x)=e^{\int -2\,\mathrm{d}x}=e^{- 2 \cdot \left(x+6\right)}.$$

Multiplying through and using the product rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(e^{- 2 \cdot \left(x+6\right)}\,z\right)=2 \cdot \left(x+6\right) \cdot e^{- 2 \cdot \left(x+6\right)}.$$

Integrating with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$e^{- 2 \cdot \left(x+6\right)}z=- \left(\left(x+6\right) + \frac{1}{2}\right) \cdot e^{- 2 \cdot \left(x+6\right)}+C.$$

Thus

$$z=C \cdot e^{2 \cdot \left(x+6\right)} - \left(x+6\right) - \frac{1}{2}.$$

Finally, substitute $z=y^{-2}$ and solve for $y$:

$$y=\pm\sqrt{- \frac{2}{- 2 \cdot C \cdot e^{2 \cdot \left(x+6\right)} + 2 \cdot \left(x+6\right) + 1}}.$$

Here $C$ is an arbitrary real constant; exclude singularities and restrict to the stated real intervals. Both signs are retained wherever the radicand is positive.

Divide by $y^{2}$ and set $z=y^{-1}$. The chain rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}=- \frac{1}{y^{2}}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.$$

Hence the linear equation in standard form is

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}+\left(3\right)z=- 3 \cdot e^{\left(x+5\right)}.$$

An integrating factor is

$$I(x)=e^{\int 3\,\mathrm{d}x}=e^{3 \cdot \left(x+5\right)}.$$

Multiplying through and using the product rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(e^{3 \cdot \left(x+5\right)}\,z\right)=- 3 \cdot e^{4 \cdot \left(x+5\right)}.$$

Finally, substitute $z=y^{-1}$ and solve for $y$:

$$y=\frac{4 \cdot e^{3 \cdot \left(x+5\right)}}{4 \cdot C - 3 \cdot e^{4 \cdot \left(x+5\right)}}.$$

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}+- \frac{4 \cdot y}{\left(x+4\right)}=- \frac{2 \cdot y^{2}}{\left(x+4\right)^{2}}. $$

Divide by $y^{2}$ and set $z=y^{-1}$. The chain rule gives

Hence the linear equation in standard form is

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}+\left(\frac{4}{\left(x+4\right)}\right)z=\frac{2}{\left(x+4\right)^{2}}.$$

An integrating factor is

$$I(x)=e^{\int \frac{4}{\left(x+4\right)}\,\mathrm{d}x}=\left(x+4\right)^{4}.$$

Multiplying through and using the product rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(\left(x+4\right)^{4}\,z\right)=2 \cdot \left(x+4\right)^{2}.$$

$$\left(x+4\right)^{4}z=\frac{2 \cdot \left(x+4\right)^{3}}{3}+C.$$

Thus

$$z=\frac{C}{\left(x+4\right)^{4}} + \frac{2}{3 \cdot \left(x+4\right)}.$$

Finally, substitute $z=y^{-1}$ and solve for $y$:

$$y=\frac{3 \cdot \left(x+4\right)^{4}}{3 \cdot C + 2 \cdot \left(x+4\right)^{3}}.$$

question.:question/problem: Find the exact solution of the equation $3^{x}=7.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We take $\log_{3}$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}3^{x}&=7\\\log_{3}(3^{x})&=\log_{3}(7)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\log_b(b^c)=c$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

$$
x=\log_{3}(7).
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=\log_{3}(7)$.

Find the exact solution of the equation $8^{x+5}=37.$

$x=$ {{solution}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we take $\log_{8}$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}8^{x+5}&=37\\\log_{8}(8^{x+5})&=\log_{8}(37)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\log_b(b^c)=c$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

$$
x+5=\log_{8}(37).
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+5&=\log_{8}(37)\\x&=\log_{8}(37)-5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=\log_{8}(37)-5$.

question.:question/problem: Given that $11^{z}=6,$ find the value of $z$ rounded to $3$ decimal places.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Taking $\log_{11}$ of both sides of the equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}
11^{z} &= 6 \\
\log_{11}\left(11^{z}\right) &= \log_{11}\left(6\right) \\
z &= \log_{11}\left(6\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we rewrite the right-hand side using the change of base formula and then solve for $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}
z &= \frac{\log(6)}{\log(11)}
\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the above on a calculator gives

$$
z\approx 0.747
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

question.:question/problem: Given that $11^{-1+4y}=\sqrt{6},$ find the value of $y$ rounded to $3$ decimal places.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Taking $\log_{11}$ of both sides of the equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}
11^{-1+4y} &= \sqrt{6} \\
\log_{11}\left(11^{-1+4y}\right) &= \log_{11}\left(\sqrt{6}\right) \\
-1+4y &= \log_{11}\left(6^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we apply the power rule to the right-hand side:

$$
-1+4y=\frac{1}{2}\log_{11}(6)
$$

Next, we rewrite the right-hand side using the change of base formula and then solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}
-1+4y &= \frac{\log(6)}{2\log(11)} \\
4y &= \frac{\log(6)}{2\log(11)}+1 \\
y &= \frac{\log(6)}{8\log(11)}+\frac{1}{4}
\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the above on a calculator gives

$$
y\approx 0.343
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

$$
\begin{aligned}
7^{-3x-2} &= \sqrt{2} \\
\log_{7}\left(7^{-3x-2}\right) &= \log_{7}\left(\sqrt{2}\right) \\
-3x-2 &= \log_{7}\left(2^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we apply the power rule to the right-hand side:

$$
-3x-2=\frac{1}{2}\log_{7}(2)
$$

Next, we rewrite the right-hand side using the change of base formula and then solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}
-3x-2 &= \frac{\log(2)}{2\log(7)} \\
-3x &= \frac{\log(2)}{2\log(7)}+2 \\
x &= -\frac{\log(2)}{6\log(7)}-\frac{2}{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the above on a calculator gives

$$
x\approx -0.726
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

question.:question/problem: Find the exact solution to the equation $4\cdot 3^{y}+12=18$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange our equation into a form that is more convenient for logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}4\cdot 3^{y}+12&=18 \\ 4\cdot 3^{y}&=6 \\ 3^{y}&=\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we take $\log_{3}$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\log_{3}\left(3^{y}\right)&=\log_{3}\left(\frac{3}{2}\right) \\ y&=\log_{3}\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $y=\log_{3}\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)$.

Now, we take $\log_{4}$ of both sides of the equation:

$$

$$

$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

question.:question/problem:

$$
2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-6y=4{e}^{4x}
$$

has the complementary solution ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{3x}$, find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation. Express your answer using only the exponentials in the forcing term.

question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation with constant coefficients on the left-hand side, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

We see that the right-hand side is $4{e}^{4x},$ and ${e}^{4x}$ is not a term in the complementary solution, so we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha {e}^{4x},
$$

where $\alpha$ is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first derivative of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=4\alpha {e}^{4x}
$$

To find the value of $\alpha ,$ we substitute ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation and group each exponential separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}(2(4\alpha )-6\alpha ){e}^{4x} &= 4{e}^{4x}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving each coefficient equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\alpha  &= \frac{4}{2} = 2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=2{e}^{4x}.
$$

The exponential $e^{2x}$ occurs in the complementary solution. An unmodified trial for that mode would give zero on the left, so multiply only that trial by $x$. The other forcing exponentials do not occur in the complementary solution. Take

$$

Differentiate, using the product rule on the resonant term:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y_p'&=\alpha (xe^{2x})'+\beta (e^{-x})'+\gamma (e^{-3x})'\\
&=\alpha (e^{2x}+2xe^{2x})-\beta e^{-x}-3\gamma e^{-3x}\\
&=\alpha (1+2x)e^{2x}-\beta e^{-x}-3\gamma e^{-3x}.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$

y_p'-2y_p&=(\alpha (1+2x)e^{2x}-\beta e^{-x}-3\gamma e^{-3x})\\
&\quad -2(\alpha xe^{2x}+\beta e^{-x}+\gamma e^{-3x})\\
&=(1+2x-2x)\alpha e^{2x}\\
&\quad +(-\beta -2\beta )e^{-x}\\
&\quad +(-3\gamma -2\gamma )e^{-3x}\\
&=\alpha e^{2x}-3\beta e^{-x}-5\gamma e^{-3x}.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{x^{5}}\left(-9 x y\,\mathrm{d}x + 6 x^{2}\,\mathrm{d}y\right)&=0 \\ -\frac{9 y^{2}}{x^{4}}\,\mathrm{d}x + \frac{6 y}{x^{3}}\,\mathrm{d}y&=0\end{aligned}
$$

For the transformed equation,

$$
P=-\frac{9 y^{2}}{x^{4}},\qquad Q=\frac{6 y}{x^{3}}.
$$

The exactness test compares the partial derivatives as functions on the region:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}&=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(-\frac{9 y^{2}}{x^{4}}\right)=-\frac{18 y}{x^{4}} \\ \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}&=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(\frac{6 y}{x^{3}}\right)=-\frac{18 y}{x^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Since

$$
\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}=\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x},
$$

the transformed equation is exact. Therefore, $I(x,y)=\frac{y}{x^{5}}$ is an integrating factor for the initial equation.

question.:question/worked-solution:
For a differential equation of the form

$$
P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y=0
$$

if

$$
\frac{1}{Q}(\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}-\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x})=g(x)
$$

where $g(x)$ is independent of $y$, an integrating factor is

$$
I(x)=\exp(\int g(x)\,\text{d}x)
$$.

Here $\exp(x)=e^x$.

Let's denote

$$
P(x,y)=- 2 x y,\qquad Q(x,y)=1
$$

Compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}&=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(- 2 x y)=- 2 x \\ \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}&=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(1)=0\end{aligned}
$$

Then

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{Q}(\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}-\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x})&=\frac{1}{1}(- 2 x-(0)) \\ &=- 2 x\end{aligned}
$$

This is a function of $x$ only. Choose the multiplicative constant to be one. Thus

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x)&=\exp(\int (- 2 x)\,\text{d}x) \\ &=\exp(- x^{2}) \\ &=e^{- x^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x)((- 2 x y)\,\text{d}x+\,\text{d}y)&=I(x)\cdot 0 \\ e^{- x^{2}}((- 2 x y)\,\text{d}x+\,\text{d}y)&=0\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:
Consider the following differential equation.

$$
y\prime=\frac{2 y}{x},\qquad x\ne 0
$$

Let $f(x)=x^{2}.$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a function $f(x)$ to be a solution to a differential equation, it must satisfy the equation for all values of $x$ in an interval where the function is defined and the equation is valid.

With that in mind, let's check each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. Differentiating $f(x)=x^{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f\prime(x)&=\left(x^{2}\right)\prime \\ &=2 x \\ &\not\equiv 5 x\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Substituting $y=x^{2}$ and $y\prime=2 x$ into the original equation gives an identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}y\prime &\overset{?}{=}\frac{2 y}{x} \\ 2 x &\overset{?}{=}\frac{2\left(x^{2}\right)}{x} \\ 2 x &=2 x\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Since statement II is true, the function $y=x^{2}$ is a solution to our differential equation.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

:question/answer-fields.:answer-field/key: II. Substituting $y=f(x)$ and $y\prime=f\prime(x)$ into the differential equation gives a true statement.
III. The function $y=f(x)$ is a solution of the differential equation.

A solution must satisfy the equation throughout the stated interval. Here $x>0$ makes the logarithm defined.

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}e^{f(x)}&=e^{3\ln x+\ln 3}\\&=e^{3\ln x}e^{\ln 3}\\&=e^{\ln(x^{3})}\cdot 3\\&=3 x^{3}.\end{aligned}

$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the following initial value problem for all real $x$:

$$

$$

question.:question/problem:

The derivatives of the proposed functions are provided:

\begin{aligned}y'&=- 2 e^{x}\\\text{RHS}&=-1\cdot \left(1 - 2 e^{x}-1\right)\\&=2 e^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

The two expressions agree throughout the interval, so this function **is a solution**.

$$
\begin{aligned}y'&=e^{x}\\\text{RHS}&=-1\cdot \left(e^{x} + 1-1\right)\\&=- e^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

At $x=1$, $y'=e$ whereas $\text{RHS}=- e$. Thus they are not identical, so this function **is not a solution**.

question.:question/problem:
Write the following first-order linear ODE in standard form.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} e^{10 x} + 3 x - 8 y e^{5 x}=0\,.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
A first-order linear ODE is in standard form if it is written as

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x).
$$

Converting the given equation to standard form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}&\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} e^{10 x} + 3 x - 8 y e^{5 x}=0 \\ &\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} e^{10 x} - 8 y e^{5 x}=- 3 x \\ &\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\underbrace{(- 8 e^{- 5 x})}_{P(x)}y=\underbrace{- 3 x e^{- 10 x}}_{Q(x)}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the equation is written in standard form with $P(x)=- 8 e^{- 5 x}$ and $Q(x)=- 3 x e^{- 10 x}.$

question.:question/problem:
Which of the following first-order linear differential equations are inhomogeneous?

Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
A first-order linear ODE is **homogeneous** if its standard form ${y}^{′}+P(x)y=Q(x)$ has $Q(x)=0$ for every $x$. It is **inhomogeneous** if $Q$ is not identically zero.

- First, we consider the equation

$$
{y}^{′}-7{x}^{3}y=-4.
$$

This equation is already in standard form. Here $Q(x)=-4$ is not identically zero, so this equation is inhomogeneous.

- Next, we consider the equation

$$
{y}^{′}-7{x}^{3}y=-2y.
$$

We move the term involving $y$ to the left, keeping the independent forcing on the right:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}-7{x}^{3}y & =-2y \\ {y}^{′}-7{x}^{3}y+2y & =0 \\ {y}^{′}-(7{x}^{3}-2)y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Here $Q(x)=0$ is identically zero, so this equation is homogeneous.

- Finally, we consider the equation

$$
{y}^{′}-7{x}^{3}y=8{x}^{3}.
$$

This equation is already in standard form. Here $Q(x)=8{x}^{3}$ is not identically zero, so this equation is inhomogeneous. Its value at $x=0$ does not determine whether it is identically zero.

Select ${y}^{′}-7{x}^{3}y=-4$; ${y}^{′}-7{x}^{3}y=8{x}^{3}$.

question.:question/problem:
Which of the following first-order linear differential equations are homogeneous?

question.:question/worked-solution:
A first-order linear differential equation is homogeneous if it can be written in the form

$$
{y}^{′}+P(x)y=0.
$$

A first-order linear differential equation is inhomogeneous if it is not homogeneous, i.e., if it can be written as

$$
{y}^{′}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

where $Q$ is not identical to zero.

To classify the equations, we examine each one in turn.

- First, we consider the equation

$$
3{y}^{′}+3{x}^{2}y-{x}^{3}=2y+{x}^{3}.
$$

We collect the $y$-terms on the left side and the terms involving only $x$ on the right side, then divide through by $3$:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{y}^{′}+3{x}^{2}y-{x}^{3} & =2y+{x}^{3} \\ 3{y}^{′}+3{x}^{2}y-2y-{x}^{3} & ={x}^{3} \\ 3{y}^{′}+(3{x}^{2}-2)y & =2{x}^{3} \\ {y}^{′}+\frac{3{x}^{2}-2}{3}y & =\frac{2{x}^{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

The forcing function is $Q(x)=\frac{2{x}^{3}}{3}$, which is not identically zero. Therefore, this equation is inhomogeneous.

- Next, we consider the equation

$$
2{y}^{′}-2y+2{x}^{3}=y+3{x}^{3}.
$$

We collect the $y$-terms on the left side and the terms involving only $x$ on the right side, then divide through by $2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{y}^{′}-2y+2{x}^{3} & =y+3{x}^{3} \\ 2{y}^{′}-2y-y+2{x}^{3} & =3{x}^{3} \\ 2{y}^{′}+(-2-1)y & ={x}^{3} \\ {y}^{′}+\frac{-2-1}{2}y & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The forcing function is $Q(x)=\frac{{x}^{3}}{2}$, which is not identically zero. Therefore, this equation is inhomogeneous.

- Finally, we consider the equation

$$
3{y}^{′}+2xy-3{x}^{3}=y-3{x}^{3}.
$$

We collect the $y$-terms on the left side and the terms involving only $x$ on the right side, then divide through by $3$:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{y}^{′}+2xy-3{x}^{3} & =y-3{x}^{3} \\ 3{y}^{′}+2xy-y-3{x}^{3} & =-3{x}^{3} \\ 3{y}^{′}+(2x-1)y & =0 \\ {y}^{′}+\frac{2x-1}{3}y & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The forcing function is $Q(x)=0$, which is identically zero. Therefore, this equation is homogeneous.

Select $3{y}^{′}+2xy-3{x}^{3}=y-3{x}^{3}$.

\begin{aligned}2{y}^{′}+3{x}^{2}y+3{x}^{3} & =2y+4{x}^{3} \\ 2{y}^{′}+3{x}^{2}y-2y+3{x}^{3} & =4{x}^{3} \\ 2{y}^{′}+(3{x}^{2}-2)y & ={x}^{3} \\ {y}^{′}+\frac{3{x}^{2}-2}{2}y & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The forcing function is $Q(x)=\frac{{x}^{3}}{2}$, which is not identically zero. Therefore, this equation is inhomogeneous.

- Next, we consider the equation

$$
3{y}^{′}+xy-4x=4y+4x.
$$

We collect the $y$-terms on the left side and the terms involving only $x$ on the right side, then divide through by $3$:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{y}^{′}+xy-4x & =4y+4x \\ 3{y}^{′}+xy-4y-4x & =4x \\ 3{y}^{′}+(x-4)y & =8x \\ {y}^{′}+\frac{x-4}{3}y & =\frac{8x}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

The forcing function is $Q(x)=\frac{8x}{3}$, which is not identically zero. Therefore, this equation is inhomogeneous.

- Finally, we consider the equation

$$
1{y}^{′}-3y-3x=3y-3x.
$$

We collect the $y$-terms on the left side and the terms involving only $x$ on the right side, then divide through by $1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}1{y}^{′}-3y-3x & =3y-3x \\ 1{y}^{′}-3y-3y-3x & =-3x \\ 1{y}^{′}+(-3-3)y & =0 \\ {y}^{′}+\frac{-3-3}{1}y & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The forcing function is $Q(x)=0$, which is identically zero. Therefore, this equation is homogeneous.

question.:question/problem: $\int 2 xe^{2 x}\,\text{d}x=$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We need to express $\int 2 xe^{2 x}\text{d}x$ as $\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =2 x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=2 \\ {v}^{′} & =e^{2 x}\, & ⟹\,v=\frac{e^{2 x}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int 2 x\cdot e^{2 x}\,\text{d}x & =2 x\cdot \frac{e^{2 x}}{2}-\int \frac{e^{2 x}}{2}\cdot 2\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2 xe^{2 x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2 xe^{2 x}-\int e^{2 x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2 xe^{2 x}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot e^{2 x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Collecting the linear terms gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2 xe^{2 x}\,\mathrm{d}x & =x e^{2 x} - \frac{e^{2 x}}{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: $\int x6^{x}\,\text{d}x=$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We need to express $\int x6^{x}\text{d}x$ as $\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′} & =6^{x}\, & ⟹\,v=\frac{6^{x}}{\ln{(6 )}}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int x\cdot 6^{x}\,\text{d}x & =x\cdot \frac{6^{x}}{\ln{(6 )}}-\int \frac{6^{x}}{\ln{(6 )}}\cdot 1\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:
Calculate $$

$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Write $I=\int 4 x\operatorname{sin}(x)\,\text{d}x$. Use integration by parts.

$$
\int uv^{\prime}\,\mathrm{d}x=uv-\int vu^{\prime}\,\mathrm{d}x.
$$

Choose the linear factor as $u$:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =4 x \\ u^{\prime} & =4 \\ v^{\prime} & =\operatorname{sin}(x) \\ v & =-\operatorname{cos}(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute into the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}uv & =4 x\left(-\operatorname{cos}(x)\right) \\ \int vu^{\prime}\,\text{d}x & =\int \left(-\operatorname{cos}(x)\right)4\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the remaining integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =-4 x\operatorname{cos}(x)+4\int \operatorname{cos}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-4 x\operatorname{cos}(x)+4(\operatorname{sin}(x))+C \\  & =-4 x\operatorname{cos}(x)+4\operatorname{sin}(x)+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the integral. Give an exact answer.

$$
\int_{0}^{1} - 3 x e^{2 x}\,\mathrm{d}x.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $I$ denote the given integral. Choose the factors so that differentiating the linear factor simplifies the remaining integral.

$$
\begin{aligned}
u&=- 3 x, & u^\prime&=-3,\\
v^\prime&=e^{2 x}, & v&=\frac{e^{2 x}}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Apply the definite integration-by-parts formula:

$$
\int_a^b uv^\prime\,\mathrm{d}x=[uv]_a^b-\int_a^b vu^\prime\,\mathrm{d}x.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=\left[- \frac{3 x e^{2 x}}{2}\right]_{0}^{1}\\
&\quad-\int_{0}^{1}\left(\frac{e^{2 x}}{2}\right)\left(-3\right)\,\mathrm{d}x,\\
&=\left[- \frac{3 x e^{2 x}}{2}\right]_{0}^{1}+\frac{3}{2}\int_{0}^{1}e^{2 x}\,\mathrm{d}x.
\end{aligned}
$$

Integrate the remaining function and combine the two primitive terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=\left[- \frac{3 x e^{2 x}}{2} + \frac{3 e^{2 x}}{4}\right]_{0}^{1}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $F(x)$ denote the primitive inside the brackets. Evaluate each endpoint, then subtract the entire lower value:

$$
\begin{aligned}
F\left(1\right)&=- \frac{3 e^{2}}{4}=- \frac{3 e^{2}}{4},\\
F\left(0\right)&=\frac{3}{4}=\frac{3}{4}.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=\left(- \frac{3 e^{2}}{4}\right)-\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)\\
&=- \frac{3 e^{2}}{4} - \frac{3}{4}.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
u&=3 x, & u^\prime&=3,\\
v^\prime&=\sin{\left(2 x \right)}, & v&=- \frac{\cos{\left(2 x \right)}}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Apply the definite integration-by-parts formula:

$$
\int_a^b uv^\prime\,\mathrm{d}x=[uv]_a^b-\int_a^b vu^\prime\,\mathrm{d}x.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=\left[- \frac{3 x \cos{\left(2 x \right)}}{2}\right]_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\\
&\quad-\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\left(- \frac{\cos{\left(2 x \right)}}{2}\right)\left(3\right)\,\mathrm{d}x,\\
&=\left[- \frac{3 x \cos{\left(2 x \right)}}{2}\right]_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}+\frac{3}{2}\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\cos{\left(2 x \right)}\,\mathrm{d}x.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}

\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
F\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)&=\frac{3}{4}=\frac{3}{4},\\
F\left(0\right)&=0=0.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
u&=3 x, & u^\prime&=3,\\

$$

$$
\int_a^b uv^\prime\,\mathrm{d}x=[uv]_a^b-\int_a^b vu^\prime\,\mathrm{d}x.

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=\left[- \frac{3 x e^{- 2 x}}{2}\right]_{\frac{1}{2}}^{1}\\
&\quad-\int_{\frac{1}{2}}^{1}\left(- \frac{e^{- 2 x}}{2}\right)\left(3\right)\,\mathrm{d}x,\\

$$
